entries.name: Academic stress
entries.response: School pressure can feel like it takes over everything.
knowledge: Deadlines can make every task feel equally urgent.
A visible plan can make a workload feel less chaotic.
Starting imperfectly is often easier than waiting to feel ready.
Rest can support concentration rather than take time away from work.
Asking for clarification early can prevent a small problem growing.
actions: List every task, then circle only the next deadline.
Turn the hardest task into a 10-minute first step.
Ask a lecturer, classmate, or tutor one specific question.
Put one short recovery break between study blocks.
questions: What part of school feels most urgent right now?
Is there one assignment or deadline worrying you most?
Have you been able to start any of the work yet?
What would make this week feel more manageable?

entries.name: Exam anxiety
phrases: i am scared of my exams
my exams are making me panic
i cannot stop thinking about results
entries.response: Exam anxiety is common, and it can make preparation feel harder than it is.
knowledge: An anxious mind often predicts the worst outcome.
Practice under gentle time limits can make an exam feel less unfamiliar.
Sleep and food can affect focus more than a last-minute all-nighter.
One exam result does not define your worth or future.
A simple plan can reduce the number of decisions you need to make.
actions: Choose one small revision topic for the next 25 minutes.
Write down what you already know before listing gaps.
Pack what you need the night before.
Use a slow exhale when panic rises during revision.
questions: When is the exam?
What part of the exam worries you most?
Are you more worried about preparation or the exam room itself?
What topic would feel most useful to review first?

entries.name: Procrastination
phrases: i cannot get myself to study
i waste time instead of working
i have no motivation to begin
entries.response: Putting something off is often a sign that the task feels too big, unclear, or emotionally uncomfortable—not that you are lazy.
knowledge: Avoiding a task can bring short relief but make pressure build later.
A task becomes easier to begin when the first action is concrete.
Motivation often follows starting rather than arriving first.
Distractions are more powerful when the next step is vague.
Progress counts even when it is smaller than you hoped.
actions: Set a five-minute timer and only open the task.
Write the first physical action, not the whole goal.
Move one distraction out of reach for a short block.
Stop after a small win and decide the next step before leaving.
questions: What task are you avoiding?
What makes it hard to start?
Would a five-minute version of it feel possible?
What usually pulls you away once you begin?

entries.name: Study burnout
phrases: i am burnt out from studying
i have no energy for coursework
entries.response: Study burnout can make even familiar work feel heavy and pointless.
knowledge: Working continuously can reduce concentration and increase mistakes.
Burnout is not always solved by pushing harder.
Recovery can include sleep, food, movement, and time away from study.
A lighter study plan may be more sustainable than an intense one.
Feeling numb about work can be a sign that you need a pause.
actions: Take a real break away from the screen for 15 minutes.
Reduce today’s plan to one essential task.
Check whether you have eaten, rested, or moved recently.
Tell someone supporting your studies that you are struggling.
questions: How long have you felt this drained?
What has your study routine been like lately?
Can you take any pressure off this week?
What would a gentler plan look like today?

entries.name: Low motivation
phrases: i do not feel like doing anything
i have no energy for anything
entries.response: Low motivation can make ordinary tasks feel much heavier than usual.
knowledge: Motivation can change with stress, sleep, routine, and mood.
Waiting to feel fully motivated can keep you stuck.
A meaningful reason can help more than pressure alone.
Tiny completed actions can rebuild momentum.
It is okay to lower the bar on a difficult day.
actions: Choose one task that takes less than five minutes.
Pair a task with something pleasant, like music or tea.
Write one reason the task matters to you.
Notice one thing you completed today, however small.
questions: When did your motivation start feeling low?
Is it affecting one area or everything?
What used to make this easier?
What is the smallest useful thing you could do next?

entries.name: Fear of failure
phrases: i am afraid of making mistakes
i am scared my results will be bad
entries.response: Fear of failure can make taking any step feel risky.
knowledge: A fear of failing can turn a challenge into a judgment about your identity.
Mistakes can show what needs adjusting, not who you are.
Other people’s expectations can make pressure feel sharper.
Trying a smaller version of a task can make risk feel manageable.
Learning rarely looks like getting everything right on the first attempt.
actions: Name the specific outcome you fear most.
Write one backup plan if the result is not what you want.
Share the worry with someone who can offer perspective.
Choose one action that improves your chances without demanding perfection.
questions: What would failure mean to you?
Whose expectations feel most present?
Have you handled a setback before?
What is one outcome you could still influence today?

entries.name: Perfectionism
phrases: nothing i do is good enough
i am too hard on myself
i need it to be flawless
i cannot stop checking my work
entries.response: Wanting to do well can be helpful, but perfectionism can make progress feel unsafe.
knowledge: High standards and self-criticism are not the same thing.
A finished draft can be improved; an avoided task cannot.
Perfectionism often moves the goalposts after you reach them.
Most work has a point where extra effort brings little benefit.
Making room for mistakes can protect your energy.
actions: Define what “good enough for today” means before starting.
Set a limit for checking or editing.
Submit a small draft to someone for feedback.
Keep one part of the task deliberately simple.
questions: What are you worried will happen if it is imperfect?
Where did this standard come from?
What would “good enough” look like here?
Is the task asking for excellence or completion right now?

entries.name: Time management
phrases: i do not have enough time
there is too much to do
i do not know where my day goes
entries.response: When there is too much competing for attention, a plan can reduce some of the mental load.
knowledge: A long unprioritized list can make every task feel urgent.
Time estimates are often more realistic after you start a task.
Leaving space between tasks helps when plans change.
A routine can reduce repeated decisions.
Rest and travel time are part of a workable schedule.
actions: Choose three priorities rather than planning every minute.
Estimate the next task, then add a small buffer.
Put one fixed commitment into a calendar first.
Review tomorrow’s plan before ending today.
questions: What is taking most of your time right now?
Which deadline is closest?
What could be delayed, shortened, or shared?
When do you usually have the best focus?

entries.name: Concentration problems
entries.response: Difficulty concentrating can be frustrating, especially when you are trying hard.
knowledge: Stress, tiredness, hunger, noise, and worry can all affect focus.
A smaller task is easier for the brain to hold in mind.
Frequent context switching can make work feel slower.
Your environment can make focus easier or harder.
Short focused periods can be more useful than forcing a long one.
actions: Put your phone out of reach for one short work block.
Choose one clear task and close unrelated tabs.
Use a timer for 15 minutes, then reassess.
Move to a quieter or more comfortable place if you can.
questions: When is focus hardest for you?
What usually distracts you first?
Have you slept and eaten recently?
Would a shorter focus block feel easier?

entries.name: General stress
phrases: i cannot cope with the stress
i feel tense all the time
entries.response: Stress can make a problem feel larger and more urgent than it actually is.
knowledge: Stress can show up in thoughts, mood, sleep, and the body.
Naming the source of pressure can make it easier to choose a next step.
Not every stressor can be removed, but some can be reduced or shared.
Short pauses can help you notice what you need.
Support is useful before stress reaches a breaking point.
actions: Name the top two sources of pressure.
Choose one thing you can postpone or ask help with.
Take three slower breaths with a longer exhale.
Do one practical task that reduces tomorrow’s pressure.
questions: What has been putting the most pressure on you?
Is the stress mostly from one area or many?
What usually helps even a little?
Who could you talk to about it?

entries.name: Overwhelm
phrases: there is too much going on
i do not know where to start
entries.response: When everything feels too much, narrowing the moment can help.
knowledge: Overwhelm can make it hard to decide what matters first.
Your brain may treat many small demands as one huge threat.
A pause can make room for a clearer next step.
You do not have to solve every problem in one moment.
Reducing choices can make action easier.
actions: Name one thing that must happen today and leave the rest for later.
Notice five things you can see around you.
Write down worries instead of carrying them all mentally.
Ask someone to sit with you while you start one task.
questions: What is demanding your attention most right now?
What can wait until tomorrow?
Are you safe and able to take a short pause?
What is the smallest next step?

entries.name: Overthinking
phrases: my mind will not switch off
entries.response: Overthinking can make uncertainty feel like an emergency that must be solved immediately.
knowledge: Thoughts can feel convincing without being facts.
Replaying a situation rarely produces a new answer after a point.
Worry can be the mind trying to protect you from uncertainty.
Putting a thought into words can make it easier to examine.
A change of attention can interrupt a worry loop.
actions: Write the worry down, then write what you actually know.
Set aside a short “worry time” later in the day.
Do a sensory activity such as a walk or shower.
Ask whether the thought is useful right now.
questions: What thought keeps returning?
Is there a trigger for the overthinking?
What do you know for certain about the situation?
What would you tell a friend with this worry?

entries.name: Self-doubt
phrases: i do not think i can do it
i am scared i cannot handle it
i do not believe in myself
entries.response: Self-doubt can make your abilities feel smaller than they are.
knowledge: Confidence is often built through evidence from small actions.
Comparing your inside experience to someone else’s outside can be misleading.
A difficult task does not prove you are incapable.
Feedback can be useful without becoming a verdict on you.
You can be unsure and still take a step.
actions: Write down one situation you handled before.
Ask for specific feedback instead of general reassurance.
Choose a task that is challenging but possible.
Replace “I cannot” with “I have not worked out how yet.”
questions: What has made you doubt yourself recently?
Is there evidence that points the other way?
What would feel like a small proof of progress?
Whose opinion feels important here?

entries.name: Low confidence
phrases: i hate how unsure i am
i do not feel confident around people
i am not comfortable with myself
entries.response: Confidence does not have to mean feeling certain all the time.
knowledge: Confidence can grow from practice, support, and keeping small promises to yourself.
Being quiet or nervous does not mean you have nothing valuable to say.
Skills improve with repetition, not only natural talent.
The way you speak to yourself can affect what you attempt.
A supportive environment can make confidence easier to build.
actions: Choose one small situation to practise speaking up.
Record one thing you did well today.
Spend time with people who treat you respectfully.
Prepare one sentence before a difficult conversation.
questions: Where does low confidence show up most?
When do you feel a little more like yourself?
What would you try if you trusted yourself more?
Who makes you feel supported?

entries.name: Sadness
phrases: i am having a bad day
entries.response: I’m sorry things feel heavy right now.
knowledge: Sadness can be a response to loss, pressure, disappointment, or something hard to name.
Feelings can shift even when the situation has not changed yet.
You do not have to explain sadness perfectly for it to deserve care.
Gentle routines can offer some steadiness on a difficult day.
Sharing a feeling can reduce isolation.
actions: Choose one comforting, low-effort activity.
Eat or drink something if you have not recently.
Tell one trusted person you are having a hard day.
Write a few words about what feels heaviest.
questions: What has been weighing on you?
Did something happen that brought this on?
Would you like to talk about it or focus on getting through today?
What support feels possible right now?

entries.name: Anger
phrases: i feel irritated all the time
entries.response: Anger often points to something that feels unfair, threatening, or repeatedly ignored.
knowledge: Anger can carry useful information, even when the reaction feels uncomfortable.
A pause can help you choose what to do with the feeling.
Stress and tiredness can lower your patience.
You can set a boundary without attacking someone.
It can help to separate what happened from what you need next.
actions: Step away briefly before replying if you can.
Name the feeling without sending a message immediately.
Move your body safely to release some tension.
Write the boundary or request you want to make.
questions: What happened just before the anger rose?
What feels unfair or hurtful here?
Do you need space before talking to anyone?
What would a calmer response protect?

entries.name: Loneliness
phrases: i feel alone even with people
i need someone to talk to
entries.response: Feeling lonely can hurt even when other people are around.
knowledge: Loneliness is about the quality of connection, not only the number of people nearby.
A low-pressure interaction can be a meaningful first step.
Many people feel lonely during transitions or changes in routine.
It can be easier to connect around a shared activity.
You deserve relationships where you can be yourself.
actions: Send one short message to someone you trust.
Spend time in a shared space, even without talking much.
Try one familiar group, class, or activity.
Make a plan for one small connection this week.
questions: When does the loneliness feel strongest?
Is there someone you miss or wish you felt closer to?
What kind of connection are you hoping for?
Would a small message to someone feel possible?

entries.name: Homesickness
phrases: i cannot adjust to this place
entries.response: Missing home can be especially hard when everything around you feels unfamiliar.
knowledge: Homesickness can happen even when you chose or wanted the move.
New routines can make a new place feel more settled over time.
Keeping a connection to home and building a connection where you are can both matter.
Transitions often take longer than people expect.
You can miss home and still make space for new experiences.
actions: Plan a call or voice note with someone from home.
Bring one familiar routine into your week.
Explore one small part of your current area.
Invite someone to do a low-pressure activity with you.
questions: What do you miss most about home?
How long have you been away?
Is there one routine from home you could keep?
Has anything started to feel familiar where you are?

entries.name: Grief and loss
phrases: i cannot get over the loss
there was a death in my family
entries.response: I’m sorry you are carrying a loss.
knowledge: Grief can come in waves and does not follow a neat timeline.
Different feelings can show up together, including sadness, anger, relief, or numbness.
Memories and anniversaries can make feelings stronger.
You do not need to grieve in the same way as anyone else.
Support can be practical as well as emotional during a loss.
actions: Let one trusted person know you are grieving.
Choose one gentle routine for today.
Write or speak a memory if that feels comforting.
Seek local bereavement or professional support if you want it.
questions: Would you like to tell me about the person or what you lost?
What has been the hardest part today?
Is there someone supporting you through this?
What would feel most caring for you right now?

entries.name: Friendship problems
phrases: i feel left out by my friends
i do not know how to talk to my friend
i feel used by my friend
entries.response: Friendship problems can feel deeply personal because they affect your sense of belonging.
knowledge: Friendships can change without either person being entirely at fault.
A clear conversation can be kinder than guessing what someone means.
It is okay to notice when a friendship feels one-sided.
Conflict does not always mean a friendship must end.
You can care about someone and still need a boundary.
actions: Write what happened before deciding what it means.
Ask for a calm conversation at a suitable time.
Use “I felt” language rather than accusations.
Reach out to another supportive person while you wait.
questions: What changed between you and your friend?
Have you been able to talk about it?
What do you need from this friendship?
Do you feel respected in it?

entries.name: Relationship problems
phrases: my partner does not understand me
i think we are drifting apart
i do not know what to do about us
entries.response: Relationship difficulties can bring up many feelings at once.
knowledge: Arguments often become worse when both people feel unheard.
A relationship can have care and still need change.
Clear requests are easier to respond to than assumptions.
You are allowed to take space before a difficult conversation.
Respect and safety are important in every relationship.
actions: Choose a calm time rather than raising it in the middle of conflict.
Name one specific issue and one specific need.
Pause the conversation if it becomes unsafe or hostile.
Talk to someone you trust for perspective.
questions: What has been hardest in the relationship lately?
Do you feel safe and respected?
What would you like to change?
Have you both had a calm chance to talk?

entries.name: Family conflict
phrases: i keep fighting with my parents
my family does not understand me
my sibling and i keep arguing
my parents are putting pressure on me
i cannot talk to my family
entries.response: Conflict at home can be draining because it can be hard to get space from it.
knowledge: Family members can care about each other and still communicate badly.
Pressure may come from worry, expectations, or unresolved conflict.
You can choose when and how to raise a difficult issue.
A boundary can be a request for space, not a rejection.
Support outside the family can help you think clearly.
actions: Wait for a calmer moment before starting a hard conversation.
Write down the main point you want to make.
Ask for one practical change rather than solving every issue.
Take a safe break from the situation if tensions rise.
questions: What is the conflict mainly about?
Do you feel safe at home?
Who in the family is easiest to talk to?
What would a better conversation look like?

entries.name: Communication problems
phrases: they do not listen to me
i do not know how to say it
i do not know how to bring it up
entries.response: Communication can break down when people feel rushed, defensive, or unheard.
knowledge: A specific example is easier to discuss than a general complaint.
Listening and agreeing are not the same thing.
Timing can change how a message lands.
Clear requests can prevent people guessing what you need.
It is okay to ask for a pause if emotions are too high.
actions: Start with one situation rather than a long history.
Use “I feel” and “I need” statements.
Ask what the other person understood before continuing.
Choose a time when neither of you is rushing.
questions: Who are you trying to communicate with?
What do you wish they understood?
What usually happens when you try to talk?
Would writing it first help you organise your thoughts?

entries.name: Social anxiety
phrases: i am scared people will judge me
i do not know what to say
i panic when i have to talk
i am afraid of embarrassing myself
entries.response: Feeling anxious in social situations can make ordinary interactions feel high-stakes.
knowledge: Anxiety can make you overestimate how closely others are judging you.
Small repeated practice can feel safer than forcing a big social event.
Preparing one opening question can reduce pressure.
Leaving a situation briefly is different from failing.
You are not required to be the most talkative person in the room.
actions: Choose one low-pressure interaction to practise.
Prepare a simple question such as “How has your week been?”
Arrive early or go with someone supportive if possible.
Give yourself permission to leave after a short time.
questions: Which social situations feel hardest?
What do you fear might happen?
Is there one person you feel more comfortable around?
What would make the next interaction 5% easier?

entries.name: Sleep problems
entries.response: Sleep difficulties can be exhausting, especially when your mind is busy.
knowledge: Stress and routines can affect sleep, but sleep problems can have many causes.
Trying hard to force sleep can sometimes increase pressure.
A predictable wind-down can help signal that the day is ending.
Bright screens and late work can keep the mind activated.
Persistent or severe sleep problems are worth discussing with a clinician.
actions: Keep the hour before bed quieter if you can.
Write tomorrow’s tasks down instead of solving them in bed.
Try a calm, low-light activity if you cannot settle.
Keep a gentle wake-up time even after a poor night.
questions: Is it harder to fall asleep, stay asleep, or wake rested?
When did the sleep problem begin?
What is your hour before bed usually like?
Is stress keeping your mind active at night?

entries.name: Work stress
phrases: i am burnt out at work
i cannot cope with my job
entries.response: Work stress can follow you beyond working hours and affect the rest of your life.
knowledge: Unclear expectations can make a workload feel heavier.
Taking a break can support better decisions at work.
Some work pressures can be discussed, delegated, or documented.
A boundary may be as small as protecting one break.
Your value is not limited to your productivity.
actions: List the tasks that are truly urgent today.
Ask for priorities when everything is labelled urgent.
Take your next break away from the work area if possible.
Write down patterns that are making work difficult.
questions: What part of work is most stressful?
Is it workload, people, hours, or something else?
Is there anyone at work you can speak to?
What boundary would help a little?

entries.name: Financial stress
phrases: i do not know how i will pay
entries.response: Money worries can make the future feel very uncertain and immediate.
knowledge: Financial stress can affect sleep, concentration, and relationships.
Looking at numbers can feel scary, but it can reveal choices.
Small practical steps can reduce uncertainty even if they do not solve everything.
You deserve support without shame.
Avoiding messages or bills can make stress grow.
actions: List the most urgent payment or deadline first.
Separate essential costs from costs that can wait.
Contact a provider early to ask what options exist.
Talk to a trusted person or local advice service if you can.
questions: What is the most urgent financial worry?
Is there a deadline coming up?
Do you have anyone safe to talk through the numbers with?
What information would help you feel less uncertain?

entries.name: Decision-making
phrases: i do not know what to choose
i am stuck between two things
i am scared to choose wrong
i do not know my next step
entries.response: A difficult decision can feel overwhelming when every option seems to carry a risk.
knowledge: Not every decision needs a perfect answer.
Values can be more useful than trying to predict everything.
Some choices can be tested rather than decided forever.
Information helps, but too much searching can increase doubt.
A deadline can help you stop reopening the same question.
actions: Write the two or three real options down.
List what matters most in this decision.
Ask what choice is reversible and what is not.
Set a time to decide after gathering enough information.
questions: What decision are you facing?
What matters most to you here?
Which option feels closer to your values?
Is any part of the decision reversible?
